questions.stem: A hospital is reviewing sharps safety after a needlestick injury. Which OSHA requirement is most relevant when an effective, clinically appropriate safer device is available?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Continue conventional sharps when annual staff training is documented, because engineering controls are optional if workers understand needlestick risks.","B":"Allow each worker to decide whether to use a safety device, because employer selection of engineering controls is not required for bloodborne-pathogen compliance.","C":"Evaluate and implement an effective, clinically appropriate safer medical device, such as a needleless system or sharp with engineered injury protection in use.","D":"Replace disposable sharps with reusable needles whenever possible, because repeated sterilization is the preferred engineering control for needlestick prevention."}}
questions.rationale: OSHA requires employers to use engineering and work-practice controls to minimize bloodborne-pathogen exposure and to evaluate and implement effective, clinically appropriate safety-engineered sharps when available. Option C states that requirement. Option A incorrectly treats training as a substitute for engineering controls. Option B incorrectly shifts the employer's control-selection obligation entirely to individual workers. Option D substitutes reusable needles for the safer-device controls OSHA describes.
questions.source_name: OSHA — Bloodborne Pathogens: Evaluating and Controlling Exposure
questions.source_detail: OSHA states that engineering and work-practice controls must minimize exposure and that an effective, clinically appropriate safety-engineered sharp must be evaluated and implemented when available.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares medication from a multidose vial. Which practice best follows CDC safe-injection guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use a new sterile needle and syringe for every entry into the vial, and dedicate the multidose vial to one patient whenever possible in clinical practice.","B":"Reuse the same needle for repeated vial entries if a new syringe is attached each time, because the needle does not need replacement until visibly soiled.","C":"Use one syringe for several patients if the needle is changed before each vial entry, because needle replacement prevents contamination of the syringe.","D":"Keep a shared multidose vial in the immediate patient-treatment area between doses, because proximity improves access without increasing contamination risk."}}
questions.rationale: CDC safe-injection guidance requires sterile single-use injection equipment and recommends single-patient dedication of multidose vials whenever possible. Option A follows both principles. Option B reuses a needle, which is unsafe even if the syringe is changed. Option C reuses a syringe across patients, which CDC prohibits even if the needle is replaced. Option D places a shared multidose vial in the immediate treatment area, where CDC guidance says it should not be kept for multi-patient use.
questions.source_detail: CDC requires a new sterile needle and syringe for each vial entry and recommends dedicating multidose vials to a single patient whenever possible.

questions.stem: A nurse performs hand hygiene before cannulating a client's arteriovenous fistula for hemodialysis. Which additional infection-prevention principle is essential?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use clean technique for fistula cannulation because bloodstream-infection prevention measures are needed only when a dialysis catheter is being accessed.","B":"Skip access-site preparation when the fistula skin appears intact, because visible cleanliness is sufficient after the nurse has completed hand hygiene.","C":"Reuse a vascular-access needle for the same client if it remains visibly clean, because repeated cannulation does not require a new sterile device each time.","D":"Use aseptic technique whenever the vascular access is cannulated and follow the facility's standardized access-care practices each time the fistula is used."}}
questions.rationale: Hand hygiene is necessary, but CDC dialysis-safety guidance also emphasizes aseptic vascular-access care and staff competency. Option D correctly adds aseptic technique and standardized access practices to hand hygiene. Option A incorrectly limits aseptic precautions to dialysis catheters. Option B skips access-site preparation based on appearance alone. Option C proposes reuse of a vascular-access needle, which is inconsistent with sterile single-use access practice.
questions.source_name: CDC — Best Practices for Bloodstream Infection Prevention in Dialysis Settings
questions.source_detail: CDC recommends staff training and competency in vascular-access care and aseptic technique and calls for observation of adherence to aseptic technique during access-related care.

questions.stem: A client arrives in cardiac arrest and requires immediate resuscitation. How should the client be classified using the Emergency Severity Index?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"ESI level 5, because this level is used for clients who need immediate life-saving intervention but are unlikely to require diagnostic resources afterward.","B":"ESI level 3, because this level is used for unstable clients requiring immediate resuscitation before the number of anticipated resources is considered.","C":"ESI level 1, because this level identifies the highest-acuity clients who require an immediate life-saving intervention such as active resuscitation.","D":"ESI level 2, because this level is assigned to cardiac arrest and other conditions after a life-saving intervention has already become necessary."}}
questions.rationale: ESI level 1 is used for the highest-acuity patients who require an immediate life-saving intervention, so a patient in cardiac arrest requiring active resuscitation is level 1. Option C is therefore correct. Option A misclassifies the patient as the lowest-acuity level. Option B assigns a middle level despite the need for immediate resuscitation. Option D assigns level 2, which is for high-risk patients who do not already meet the level-1 life-saving-intervention criterion.
questions.source_name: Emergency Nurses Association — Emergency Severity Index Handbook, 5th Edition
questions.source_detail: Current ENA ESI resources describe a five-level triage scale and identify Decision Point A as whether a life-saving intervention is required; life-saving interventions meet ESI level 1 criteria.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old seeks testing and treatment for a suspected sexually transmitted infection and asks whether parental consent is required. Which response is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Federal law requires parental consent for every STI service provided to a minor, so testing or treatment cannot begin until a parent signs authorization.","B":"All states and the District of Columbia allow minors to consent to STI services, although age, confidentiality, or notification provisions can vary by jurisdiction.","C":"Minors may consent to STI testing but not treatment in any state, so a parent must authorize medication even when the adolescent requested the evaluation.","D":"Minor consent for STI services applies only after emancipation, because non-emancipated adolescents cannot independently consent to this care without a parent present."}}
questions.rationale: CDC states that minors can consent to their own STI services in all 50 states and the District of Columbia, while some age, notification, and confidentiality provisions vary. Option B accurately separates the consent rule from jurisdiction-specific details. Option A incorrectly states that parental consent is universally required. Option C incorrectly separates testing from treatment as a universal rule. Option D incorrectly limits minor consent to emancipated adolescents.
questions.source_detail: CDC states that all 50 states and the District of Columbia explicitly allow minors to consent for their own STI services; age provisions for some services and confidentiality or notification issues can vary by jurisdiction.
